sweep_summary: Kera (kera1255) is in the catalog as no-word-stress on Pearce 2006 (Phonology). The sweep's four title hits are three Pearce works and one misassigned JASA paper. The 2007 UCL thesis (already on file, read: pp.27, 60, 92, 191, 333) states first-hand that overt stress plays no role and no syllable is more intense than the others, with prominence only at the head of iambic feet: confirms the catalog. The 2006 article's Crossref abstract ('Kera has no word-level stress') matches the catalog quote verbatim; its full text is paywalled and the archived author copy could not be re-fetched sources (Internet Archive offline during the sweep). The 2013 CSLI book is the print version of the thesis (Harvard offsite only). Newman 2003 (JASA) is an English VOT/fricative study attached to Kera by a Glottolog machine assignment from the word 'evaluate': irrelevant. Extra: the catalog's secondary source Pearce 2007 ACAL 37 'Iambicity in Kera' was fetched sources open from Cascadilla and also confirms (p.66: no overt stress in pitch or intensity; iambic feet with heavy heads). Pearce 2005 CamLing 'Iambicity without stress in Kera' remains unlocated. No change to the catalog coding is warranted; the thesis can be added as a co-equal primary corroborating source. new_statements.quote: Traditionally, the cue which is used the most as evidence for foot structure is the stress placed on head vowels. In Kera, stress is not particularly noticeable, and there is no pattern where one syllable is more intense than all the others giving rise to a word accent. Nevertheless, intensity is used at the level of the foot and this can be measured. The intensity is greater for the head of the foot. There is a consistent difference between heads and non-heads.
new_statements.citation: Pearce, Mary Dorothy (2007). The interaction of tone with voicing and foot structure: evidence from Kera phonetics and phonology. PhD thesis, University College London.
new_statements.reading: Kera has no word-level stress or word accent; there is foot-level prominence only (the head of each quantity-sensitive iambic foot is longer, more intense and has distinct vowel allophones), which is exactly the catalog's 'no-word-stress' coding. This is the full-length first-hand treatment behind the catalog's deciding 2006 Phonology article, by the same author and with the same instrumental evidence.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: all deciding segments found verbatim at the stated pages in the held Pearce 2006 text; the dq (domain) passage at p.269 also verbatim. (2) The classification rests on a 2006 peer-reviewed phonology article with instrumental data by the language's main specialist, corroborated by her held 409-pp 2007 PhD, which repeats 'no overt stress at the word level' in at least five places; this is the best available description of Kera prosody per the Glottolog bibliography (the only higher-page-count item, Ebert 1979, is an older impressionistic grammar). (3) The one substantive gap is that Ebert 1979:58 — the source of StressTyp2's contradictory 'leftmost heavy else final' coding — is held only as StressTyp2's paraphrase; it is print-only and would document the conflict first-hand but not overturn a coding based on later acoustic work that cites Ebert. sources.citation: Pearce, Mary Dorothy (2007). The interaction of tone with voicing and foot structure: evidence from Kera phonetics and phonology. PhD thesis, University College London, xiii+409 pp. [Glottolog 15175]
sources.quote: [p.27] In most languages, any discussion of the foot structure will focus on the positioning of stress in the language. However, I cannot use stress as an indicator of the structure, because overt stress does not play a major role in the Kera system. [p.60] Traditionally, the cue which is used the most as evidence for foot structure is the stress placed on head vowels. In Kera, stress is not particularly noticeable, and there is no pattern where one syllable is more intense than all the others giving rise to a word accent. Nevertheless, intensity is used at the level of the foot and this can be measured. The intensity is greater for the head of the foot.
sources.locator: ch. 2 'Foot structure', sec. 2.1 p.27; sec. 2.2.4 'Intensity' p.60; also p.92, p.191, p.333
sources.note: First-hand, instrumental: Kera has no word-level stress/word accent; no syllable is more intense than all others. What exists is quantity-sensitive iambic foot structure whose heads carry greater intensity, duration and [-ATR] vowel allophony; the foot is the domain of vowel harmony and tone spreading and, in 3+-syllable words, the tone-bearing unit. p.92: 'Kera is unusual in being an example of an iambic language where stress has no role to play in the parsing of feet'; p.191: 'even without overt stress at the word level'.

sources.citation: Pearce, Mary (2007). Iambicity in Kera. In D. L. Payne & J. Peña (eds), Selected Proceedings of the 37th Annual Conference on African Linguistics, 66-76. Somerville, MA: Cascadilla. [catalog secondary source, not in target list; fetched sources]
sources.quote: Although Afro-asiatic tone languages typically do not exhibit overt stress in the form of higher pitch or greater intensity, this paper will consider the evidence for a metrical system in Kera (an Eastern Chadic tone language spoken in southern Chad and parts of Cameroon, with 50,000 speakers (Ebert 1979; Pearce 1998, 2003, 2005, 2006)). Iambic feet are constructed over a combination of light and heavy syllables with an obligatory heavy syllable for the head of the foot.
sources.note: No overt stress (pitch or intensity) at word level; iambic feet with obligatory heavy heads, evidenced by vowel deletion/lengthening, allophony, harmony and tone spreading.
